We need to assign a value to the four different cases (see Figure 1C). For example, in our movie-goer scenario, it would make sense to assign a positive value β to giving a flyer to a complier (because we gain a customer), a small negative value γ to an always-goer and θ to a never-goer (because we wasted the flyer on them), and a larger negative value δ to a defier (because we lost a customer). Based on these values, we can then compute the expected benefit of handing out the flyer, like so where we've written out the different types of people following the notation in prior work (Angrist et al., 1996; Li & Pearl, 2022; Mueller & Pearl, 2023; Tian & Pearl, 2000).

For example, the probability of being a complier, p(y x , y ′ x ′ ), is the probability that a person would get a ticket (y) if they got a flyer (x) but wouldn't get a ticket (y ′ ) if they didn't get a flyer (x ′ ). So, to make good decisions, we need to estimate the probability of the four different types of people, assign a value to each type, compute the expected benefit, and act accordingly. 1While we generally benefit from having both experimental and observational data, there are some conditions where having observational data in addition to experimental data doesn't help. This is the case when either monotonicity (Angrist et al., 1996) or gain equality holds (Li & Pearl, 2019). Monotonicity means that the probability of being a defier is 0 (i.e., there are no movie-goers who were discouraged by the flyer -people who would have gone had they not received it). In other words, it's not possible for a change from x ′ to x to lead to a change from y to y ′ . If p(defier) = 0, then this means that p(y x ) -p(y x ′ ) = p(complier) (see Equation 3), so all we need to know is the average treatment effect based on the experimental data alone. Gain equality holds when the benefit of selecting a complier and a defier is equivalent to the benefit of selecting an always-goer and a never-goer. In other words, gain equality is satisfied when β + δ = γ + θ in Equation 6.

A worked example

To illustrate how the model works, let's consider the data from 'Zeus Theater' in Figure 1A again. Our first goal is to determine the probability of the four counterfactual types of people who go to 'Zeus Theater'. Let's start with computing the probability that someone is a complier (see Equation 1). To do so, we need the experimental and observational data. The experimental study at 'Zeus Theater' establishes that p(y x ) = 0.7 and p(y x ′ ) = 0.5. If that were all we had, then we could use Equation 1 to determine that the probability of someone being a complier is within the following range: max{0, 0.2} ≤ p(complier) ≤ min{0.7, 0.5}. So the chance of someone being a complier is between 20% and 50%. Notice that to determine the bounds here, we simply dropped all of the terms that have observational probabilities from Equation 1.

In the observational data, the probability of a movie-goer taking a flyer of their own accord is p(x) = 0.5 as half of the movie-goers took a flyer and the other half didn't. We can compute the observational probabilities we need for Equation 1 in the following way: p(x, y) = p(y|x) • p(x) = 0.4 •0.5 = 0.2, p(x ′ , y) = 0, p(x, y ′ ) = 0.3, p(x ′ , y ′ ) = 0.5, and p(y) = p(x, y) + p(x ′ , y) = 0.2. If all we had was this observational data, we would infer that max{0} ≤ p(complier) ≤ min{0.7}. So, based on the observational data only, we would infer that the probability of someone being a complier is between 0% and 70%.

Based on the information from the experimental data and observational data considered separately, we know already that the probability of someone being a complier must be between 20% and 50%. But, as it turns out, we can do better than that. By combining both experimental and observational data, we get the following: max{0, 0.2, -0.3, 0.5} ≤ p(complier) ≤ min{0.7, 0.5, 0.7, 0.5}. So, by combining both sources of the data, we get a point estimate of the probability that someone is a complier. Here, there is exactly a 50% chance that someone is a complier.

From p(complier) = 0.5 and p(y x ) = 0.7, we can compute p(always-goer) = 0.2 (using Equation 2), because there are only two ways a person with the flyer ends up going to the theater: they are either a complier or an always-goer. Knowing that the average treatment effect is p(y x ) -p(y x ′ ) = 0.2 and that p(complier) = 0.5, we can compute p(defier) = 0.3 (using Equation 3). Finally, from p(defier) = 0.3 and p(y ′ x ) = 0.3, we can compute p(never-goer) = 0 (using Equation 4).

Again, there are only two ways that someone with the flyer would not go to the theater: they must either be a defier or a never-goer. So, based on the observational and experimental data, there is a 50% chance that someone is a complier, a 20% chance that they are an always-goer, a 30% chance they are a defier, and a 0% chance a never-goer. Now that we know the probability of the four different types, we need to assign a value for each of them to decide whether it's worth handing out the flyer (Figure 1C). Let's assume that the cost of handing out the flyer is $0.50, and that the reward of giving the flyer to a complier is $10. The cost of handing the flyer to a defier is $20. Assume this is due to a lost profit of $10 and a $10 damage to the theater's reputation for recommending a movie that turned a customer away. So, taking into account the cost of the flyer, we get the following values for the different types of movie-goers shown in Figure 1C: Mary the complier (β = $9.50), Jerry the always-goer (γ = -$0.50), Larry the never-goer (θ = -$0.50), and Carrie the defier (δ = -$20.50). Putting the values and probabilities into Equation 6, we get: expected benefit = $9.50 • 0.5 -$0.50 • 0.2 -$0.50 • 0 -$20.50 •0.3 = -$1.50. So, it's not worth handing out flyers at 'Zeus Theater' (see Figure 1D). We expect to lose $1.50 in value per customer by handing out flyers compared to not handing out flyers. This example illustrates that we can make better decisions by integrating both experimental and observational data, rather than relying on either data source alone. Now, we will examine how people make decisions, and whether they follow the CDM's normative predictions.

Experiment 1: Decisions with and without feedback

In this experiment, participants viewed situations like the ones in Figure 1A and had to decide whether or not to hand a flyer to a movie-goer from that theater. Between conditions, we manipulated whether participants received feedback about their choices. We explore to what extent participants' decisions are predicted by the CDM versus alternative models, and whether receiving feedback affects their performance.

Methods

All three experiments in this paper were pre-registered. You can access the preregistrations, experiment demos, data, materials, statistical analyses and an interactive visualization of the CDM at https://github.com/cicl-stanford/good_decisions. All experiments were approved by Stanford's Institutional Review Board (IRB #48665).

Participants

We recruited 199 participants via Prolific (age: M = 35 years, SD = 12; gender: 116 female, 79 male, 2 non-binary, 2 undisclosed; race: 162 White, 13 Black, 12 Asian, 5 Hispanic, 2 American Indian/Alaska Native, 1 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 1 Multiracial, 3 undisclosed). Participants received a base payment of $2.50 and an initial bonus of $1. Whenever they handed out the flyer, their bonus changed by that trial's benefit in Table 1 divided by 10, and declining to hand it out left their bonus unchanged. For example, handing out the flyer on trial 1 would cost them 55 cents, and handing it out on trial 22 would earn them 35 cents. Making every decision correctly would bring their bonus to $2.55, and making every decision incorrectly would in principle bring it to -$1.90. However, the bonus could not fall below $0.

Design

Participants were assigned to the 'feedback' condition (N = 100) or 'no feedback' condition (N = 99). Participants saw 22 trials where the information was presented just like in Figure 1A. Each scenario took place at a different movie theater. In each scenario, participants saw experimental data (randomly chosen movie-goers were handed a flyer) and observational data (movie-goers chose whether to take a flyer). We randomized the trial order between participants. The trials varied the experimental and observational data (see Table 1). 1 Experimental data is represented by the number of movie-goers who returned to watch the movie, separately for those who were handed a flyer and those who weren't. Observational data is represented the same way, separately for those who took a flyer and those who didn't. We chose these scenarios with the following considerations in mind. We wanted a range of situations that differed in their expected benefit. We wanted to have the same number of trials with positive and negative expected benefit. And we wanted to have situations where the experimental probabilities were held constant, but the observational data differed in a way that affected whether the expected benefit was positive or negative.

Procedure

All participants read a set of instructions about the task, saw an example trial, and answered comprehension questions. Participants were only allowed to proceed if they answered all comprehension questions correctly. If a participant answered one or more questions incorrectly, the instructions were presented again. Among other aspects of the task, the comprehension questions made sure that participants understood the difference between the experimental and the observational data (see Appendix A for the full set of questions).

Participants learned about a movie theater company that is testing out advertisements (flyers) for a new movie at various theater locations. Depending on the movie-goer, a flyer may encourage, discourage, or have no effect on whether the movie-goer will see the movie. Participants learned that a movie-goer who returns to see the advertised movie because of the flyer results in $10 of profit. A movie-goer who doesn't return to see the advertised movie because of the flyer incurs a loss of $20 due to lost profit and damaged reputation. The cost of a flyer is $0.50. Hence, the associated benefits of compliers (β), always-goers (γ), never-goers (θ), and defiers (δ) are $9.50, -$0.50, -$0.50, and -$20.50, respectively. On each trial, participants' task was to decide whether or not to hand out a flyer to a new potential customer at the current theater. For example, we asked "Do you want to hand Marcus a flyer?", and participants responded by clicking a "yes" or "no" button. Participants were asked about a new individual at a new theater on each trial.

In the 'no feedback' condition, participants immediately proceeded to the next trial after having chosen their response. In the 'feedback' condition, participants learned whether their decision was correct, what their bonus in this round was, and what their bonus would have been had they chosen differently. For example, if a participant decided to hand out the flyer on trial 1, they received feedback that their choice was incorrect, that they lost 55 cents this round, and that they would have lost 0 cents if they hadn't handed out the flyer. If a participant decided not to hand out the flyer on trial 3, they received feedback that their choice was correct, that their bonus for this round was 0 cents, and that they would have lost 35 cents if they had handed out the flyer.

On the first two trials, participants viewed the data with a textual description first before making their decision. For example, participants were told that "0 out of 10 moviegoers who took the flyer went to see the movie, . . . " (observational data) and that "5 out of 10 movie-goers who were given the flyer went to see the movie, . . . " (experimental data). This was done to further ensure that participants understood how to read the data. The order of these first two trials was fixed (the first trial was trial 1, and the second trial was trial 10 from Table 1). After that, participants just viewed the data without any textual descriptions, and the trials were presented in random order.

At the end of the experiment, we asked what factors influenced their decisions and whether they had any other thoughts or comments about the experiment. Participants also provided demographic information. It took participants an average of 14 minutes (SD = 7) to complete the experiment.

Results

Figure 2 shows the results for a selection of six scenarios from the experiment. The top row shows the different scenarios, and the bottom row shows the percentage of participants who chose to hand out the flyer on each trial in the different experimental conditions. (You can ignore the middle row of the plot for now.) Scenarios A and B have the same experimental data but different observational data. In scenario A, the correct decision is not to hand out the flyer, as the expected benefit is -$1.50. In the 'no feedback' condition, 37% of participants handed out the flyer, and 53% of participants did so in the 'feedback' condition. In scenario B, the correct decision is to hand out the flyer. The majority of participants in both conditions chose to do so with 79% in the 'no feedback' condition, and 71% in the 'feedback' condition. This comparison illustrates that participants weren't making their decisions solely based on the experimental data. That said, participants struggled to integrate the observational data as prescribed by the CDM. For example, in scenario C, the expected benefit is the same as in scenario B, even though the observational data is quite different. However, participants were much less likely to hand out the flyer in scenario C compared to scenario B.

sources of evidence, consider scenarios D and E. The expected benefit of both scenarios is the same (-$0.50), so participants should not hand out the flyer. However, participants' decisions differ strongly between the two cases. In scenario D, 17% of participants in the 'no feedback' condition, and 14% in the 'feedback' condition handed out the flyer. In contrast, in scenario E, 56% of participants chose to do so in the 'no feedback' condition, and 51% in the 'feedback' condition. Participants' responses are intuitive here. Just like in scenarios A-C, the experimental data is identical in both scenarios D and E. The only thing that differs is the observational data. In scenario D, no one who took the flyer in the observational study bought a ticket, and everyone who didn't take the flyer bought a ticket. In scenario E, the observational data is completely flipped. Nonetheless, it turns out that the expected benefit is the same in both situations. The combination of both data sources implies that half of the people at each theater are always-goers, and the other half are never-goers. So we would be wasting our flyer in both scenarios. The difference in observational data is due to the always-goers not picking up a flyer (there's no need) and never-goers picking up a flyer (maybe they're hoping to have their minds changed) in scenario D, and the always-goers picking up a flyer (maybe they're excited about the movie) and never-goers not picking up a flyer (there's no need) in scenario E. Scenario F shows a case in which the majority of participants made the correct decision. In each condition, 77% of participants handed out the flyer. This is the scenario with the highest expected benefit of $3.50 (see Table 1).

Figure 3 shows how much bonus participants received in each condition. The expected bonus for random responding is $0.325. Participants' average bonus exceeded the chance level in both the 'no feedback' condition (Mean = 0.51, 95% confidence interval = [0.37, 0.64]) and the 'feedback' condition (0.55, [0.44, 0.68]). There was no credible difference between how much bonus participants received in the two conditions (see Table C1). In the 'no feedback' condition, 62% of participants received a bonus above the chance level, and 64% in the 'feedback' condition. Participants' decisions in both conditions were highly correlated, r = .94.

Overall, participants in the 'no feedback' condition made the correct decision 54% [51%, 56%] of the time. Participants in the 'feedback' condition chose correctly 55% [53%, 57%] of the time. Participants in the 'feedback' condition did not make better decisions over time. Participants were more likely to hand out the flyer than not, both in the 'no feedback' condition (56%, [53%, 58%]) and in the 'feedback' condition (56%, [54%, 58%]). Remember that we had chosen the trials so that, for half of them, it was the correct decision not to hand out a flyer (trials 1-11 in Table 1), and to hand it out for the other half (trials 12-22).

To better understand how participants made their decisions, we compared their decisions to the predictions of five different models (see Table 2). The CDM computes the expected benefit by combining the experimental and observational data in a non-linear way as described above. The other models use linear combinations of the experimental and observational data to predict participants' decisions. Figure 4 shows scatterplots of model predictions and participants' choices across the 22 trials. Because the models differ in their Table 2 Models of participants' decisions. Discussion

Participants had trouble using both experimental and observational data to make good decisions. While they performed better than chance on average, performance was far from optimal. Interestingly, participants' performance wasn't much better when they received feedback, and didn't improve over time in the feedback condition. Integrating the two sources of data as prescribed by the CDM is not something that comes naturally to people. In the words of one of our participants: "It doesn't feel consistent. There were two sets of almost identical data; I chose one answer, got it wrong, then choose the other and got it wrong again." Even though participants' decisions didn't follow the CDM, their answers were very systematic. Some participants explicitly mentioned focusing on one side of the data, observational (e.g., "I looked at how many [movie-goers] came back if flyers were available.") or experimental (e.g., "I looked at how many [movie-goers] who returned were given fliers."). Overall, the 'full' model, which combines the information from both experimental and observational studies in a weighted additive way, captured participants' decisions best (see Table 3).

Experiment 2: Inferring counterfactual types before making decisions

In Experiment 1, we found that people had trouble integrating experimental and observational data to make optimal decisions. In Experiment 2, we wanted to see whether people can estimate the probability of the different counterfactual types (complier, alwaysgoer, etc.) based on the data, and whether being asked to do so would improve performance. We also asked another group of participants to report the data itself before making decisions, to see whether any potential improvement was due specifically to thinking about the counterfactual types, or merely due to being asked to pay closer attention to the data.

Methods

Participants

We recruited 102 participants via Prolific (age: M = 36 years, SD = 12; gender: 56 female, 42 male, 2 non-binary, and 2 undisclosed; race: 84 White, 6 Black, 10 Asian, 1 Hispanic, and 1 undisclosed). Participants were compensated at a base rate of $10 per hour, with a maximum rate of $17.10 per hour depending on performance. Of the 102 participants, 48 were assigned to the 'data composition' condition and 54 to the 'people inference' condition.

Design and procedure

The design and procedure of Experiment 2 were largely identical to those of the 'feedback' condition in Experiment 1. However, this time, participants in the 'people inference' condition were asked to assess the composition of the four types of people in each theater prior to choosing whether or not to hand out a flyer. On each trial, participants were asked to estimate percentages of people at this movie theater and enter their estimates in text boxes next to the four labels "encouraged to go by the flyer", "would go with or without the flyer", "would not go with or without the flyer", and "discouraged to go by the Table 3 Model comparison for each experimental condition. r = Pearson correlation, RMSE = root mean squared error (computed on the trial averages), CDM = counterfactual decision model. ∆elpd shows the difference in expected log predictive density using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation between the best-fitting model (indicated by 0) and the other models, along with associated standard error. Larger negative numbers indicate worse performance (see Vehtari, Gelman, & Gabry, 2017, for details). no feedback feedback data composition people inference (novice) people inference (expert) Model r RMSE ∆elpd r RMSE ∆elpd r RMSE ∆elpd r RMSE ∆elpd r RMSE ∆elpd Experimental .49 0.17 -355 (23.3) .62 0.13 -179.7 (17.8) .64 0.16 -122.5 (14.8) .51 0.17 -157.6 (15.7) .77 0.18 -115.2 (14.3) Observational .90 0.12 -53.4 (10.5) .84 0.10 -44.7 (9.8) .86 0.12 -23.1 (7.4) .92 0.10 -12.2 (5.4) .80 0.17 -94 (13.2) Full .97 0.10 0 (0) .97 0.06 0 (0) .96 0.09 0 (0) .98 0.07 0 (0) .98 0.07 0 (0) ∆P combined .79 0.13 -220.8 (18.7) .88 0.08 -92.2 (13.2) .91 0.10 -21.6 (7.8) .87 0.11 -58.1 (10.1) .98 0.06 -0.1 (5.1) CDM .25 0.19 -394.3 (24.1) .35 0.15 -213.4 (18.6) .58 0.17 -124.6 (15.9) .50 0.17 -154.1 (15.7) .69 0.20 -142.5 (15.5) flyer".

The input boxes were limited to numbers from 0 to 100, and participants could only proceed if the numbers they entered into the four boxes added up to 100. In the 'data composition' condition, participants were asked to enter the number of people who returned to the theater under each condition. Participants put in a number between 0 and 10 next to the four labels "took flyer (top right cell)", "did not take flyer (bottom right cell)", "were given flyer (top left cell)", and "were not given flyer (bottom left cell)".

On the same screen, participants in both conditions were also asked to choose whether or not to hand out a flyer. In the 'data composition' condition, participants were only able to proceed to the next screen if they had entered all of the four data values correctly (and after having decided whether or not to hand out a flyer). After their decision, participants received feedback in the same way as in Experiment 1's 'feedback' condition.

We made one small change in the order in which the trials were presented. Because all participants received feedback now, we wanted it to be the case that among the first two trials, the correct decision was to hand out the flyer in one of them, and not in the other. So participants always saw trial 12 first, and then trial 10 second (see Table 1). The order for the rest of the trials was randomized. Participants took an average of 29 minutes (SD = 14) to complete the experiment.

Results

We will first discuss participants' inferences in the 'people inference' condition, then their decisions in both conditions of the experiment, and finally the relationship between people inferences and decisions.

People inference task

The middle row of Figure 2 shows participants' inferences for a selection of trials together with the predictions of the CDM (Table B1 shows the inferences for all trials).

For example, in scenario A, the CDM predicts that there is a 50% chance that a person is a complier, a 20% chance they are an always-goer, a 0% chance a never-goer, and a 30% chance a defier. Participants' averaged judgments differed from these predictions. They considered it roughly equally likely that a person was a complier or an always-goer, and unlikely that they were a never-goer or a defier. For scenarios B and C, the CDM predicts the same inference. However, people's inferences differed markedly between the two scenarios. They were more likely to believe that a person is a complier than an always-goer in scenario B, but the opposite is true for scenario C. In scenarios D and E, the CDM again predicts the same inference, but people's inferences differed. In scenario D, participants considered it likely that the person could be a defier, whereas the CDM considers that impossible. In scenario F, people's inferences are more closely aligned with the predictions of the CDM.

Table 4 shows what aspects of the data most strongly affected participants' inferences. We ran separate Bayesian linear mixed effects models for each person type (complier, always-goer, never-goer, and defier), using the experimental and observational data as predictors. We find that participants' judgments of whether someone is a complier are most strongly affected by the proportion of people who bought a ticket after having taken the flyer in the observational study, p(y|x). This is also true for people's judgments about nevergoers and defiers, although here the relationship is negative. For always-goers, participants' judgments are most strongly affected by the proportion of people who bought a ticket even though they didn't pick up a flyer, p(y|x ′ ). 1 So while participants paid attention to the different sources of information, they weren't able to reliably infer the probability of the four counterfactual types across the trials. The correlation between the CDM's predictions and participants' inferences was r = .11 [-.10, .31].

Decision task

Figure 2 shows participants' decisions for a selection of trials. For most of these trials, the majority of participants made the same decisions as in Experiment 1. The correlation between participants' decisions in the two Experiment 2 conditions was r(people inference, data composition) = .69 (see Table D1).

Figure 3 shows that participants performed slightly better in Experiment 2 than in Experiment 1. In the 'people inference' condition, participants' average bonus was 0.81 [0.62, 0.99], and in the 'data composition' condition, it was 0.89 [0.69, 1.08]. In each of the 'people inference' and 'data composition' conditions, 81% of participants received a bonus above the chance level. Participants received credibly more bonus in the 'people inference' and 'data composition' conditions than in both Experiment 1 conditions (see Table C1). However, there was no credible difference in performance between the 'people inference' and the 'data composition' condition. Overall, participants in the 'people inference' condition decided correctly 58% [55%, 62%] of the time, and 59% [55%, 62%] of the time in the 'data composition' condition. Just like in Experiment 1, participants were more likely to 1 Notice that fitting a linear model based on the experimental and observational data to predict the true probability of the counterfactual types according to the CDM yields only moderate correlations, illustrating that these inferences cannot simply be achieved through a linear combination of features: r(complier) = .47, r(always-goer) = .50, r(never-goer) = .50, r(defier) = .42. Relationship between people inference and decisions. Scatterplots show the relationship between the empirical expected benefit computed from participants' people inferences, and the probability with which participants handed out the flyer. A shows the results for novices and B for experts. Each point shows one of the 22 trials. Note: The error bars show 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. The labels refer to the scenarios shown in Figure 2.

hand out the flyer than not, doing so 54% [51%, 56%] of the time in the 'people inference' condition, and 57% [54%, 59%] of the time in the 'data composition' condition. Just like in the 'feedback' condition in Experiment 1, participants' decisions did not improve across trials despite receiving feedback. There was neither an effect of trial number on whether a decision was correct in the 'people inference' condition, -0.02 [-0.03, 0.00], nor in the 'data composition' condition, -0.01 [-0.03, 0.01].

When comparing participants' decisions to the predictions of the CDM and alternative models (Table 3), we see again that the 'full' model captured participants' decisions best while the CDM performed much less well (see also Figure 4).

Relationship between people inferences and decisions

We saw that neither participants' people inferences nor their decisions are wellpredicted by the CDM. However, participants' (incorrect) people inferences were closely related to their decisions. Figure 5 shows a very close relationship between the empirical expected benefit (computed from participants' inferences) and their decisions. To compute the empirical expected benefit, we took the averaged judgments for the four person types and multiplied them by the benefit for each type, as prescribed by Equation 6. For example, in scenario A of Figure 2, participants' averaged inferences were the following: p(complier) = 0.37, p(always-goer) = 0.41, p(never-goer) = 0.13, p(defier) = 0.08, so the empirical expected benefit for this trial would be: $9.50 • 0.37 -$0.50 • 0.41 -$0.50 • 0.13 -$20.50 •0.08 = $1.60. Notice that the actual expected benefit for this scenario, according to the CDM, is -$1.50. The majority of participants decided to hand out flyers, which is in line with the empirical expected benefit but not the actual expected benefit.

Discussion

Having participants engage more closely with the experimental and observational data led to slightly improved decisions compared to those of Experiment 1. Even though participants did better in this experiment, their decisions were still only moderately correlated with the CDM's predictions (see Table 3). While performance was higher this time compared to Experiment 1, it didn't improve over time, suggesting that participants were unable to improve their decision-making strategy with feedback.

In the 'people inference' condition, we found that participants' inferences were not well-predicted by the CDM. Instead, participants' inferences were well-captured by a model that assumes a linear weighting of the observational and experimental probabilities (see Table 4). Furthermore, there was a highly systematic relationship between participants' inferences and their decisions. The greater the expected benefit based on their people inferences, the more likely they were to hand out the flyer (see Figure 5).

Experiment 3: Expert judgments

Experiments 1 and 2 tested non-expert participants who were recruited via Prolifican online crowdsourcing platform. We found that the counterfactual inferences and decisions of these participants weren't well-captured by the CDM. In this experiment, we tested expert participants. Most people rarely make decisions based on covariation data from observational and experimental studies. However, data scientists, statisticians, doctors, and consultants have ample experience with this kind of data and regularly make highstakes decisions based on it. Therefore, it is important to know whether their inferences and decisions correspond more closely to the predictions of the CDM. We recruited students and postdocs who study statistics, economics, or data science at Stanford University and gave them the same task as participants in the 'people inference' condition in Experiment 2. We hypothesized that experts' inferences about the different counterfactual types would be more accurate than those of novices, and that experts would make better decisions, too.

Methods

Participants

We recruited 53 participants by advertising the study on department email lists (age: M = 23 years, SD = 4; gender: 26 female, 26 male, 1 non-binary; race: 26 White, 21 Asian, 3 Black/African American, and 3 Other; ethnicity: 3 Hispanic, 50 Non-Hispanic; degree: 27 undergraduate students, 1 Master's student, 22 PhD students, 3 postdocs). Participants received an Amazon gift voucher worth $20 as base payment plus a performance-related bonus of up to $10.20.

Design and procedure

The design and procedure were identical to the 'people inference' condition in Experiment 2. This time, we collected more demographic data at the end of the study, including information about their degree, their department, their area of study, and their familiarity with causal inference.foot_4

Results

Figure 2 shows participants' inferences and decisions for a subset of trials. Overall, experts' inferences and decisions were similar to those of novices. However, in scenario A, experts misjudged the proportion of every counterfactual type by more than novices did, yet they were somewhat less likely to hand out the flyer, which was the correct decision in this scenario. In scenario E, the experts were more accurate in their inferences and less likely not to hand out the flyer, which was the correct decision.

People inferences

Contrary to what we predicted, experts were not better than novices at inferring the counterfactual types. For each participant and trial, we computed the squared error between their people inference and the CDM's predictions. We then looked at whether the errors were smaller for experts compared to novices. In fact, experts had slightly higher errors in their inferences compared to novices, although this difference was not credible (100.60, 95% CrI [-2.10, 203.69]). Across all of the 22 trials, the novice and expert inferences were strongly correlated (r = .75, RMSE = 0.08), but expert inferences were less correlated with the normative inferences compared to novices (novices: r = .11, RMSE = 0.22; experts: r = .06, RMSE = 0.23).

Table 4 shows what information experts relied on when making their inferences. There were a few notable differences between experts and novices. First, when inferring the probability of compliers, experts put more weight on the experimental data for the group that didn't get the flyer, p(y x ′ ). Second, when inferring the probability of never-goers, they put more weight on the experimental data for the group that got the flyer, p(y x ). Finally, when inferring the probability of defiers, they put more weight on the observational data for the group that didn't take the flyer, p(y|x ′ ).

Decisions

As predicted, experts made better decisions than novices. Table 1 shows that experts were more often correct than novices, and Figure 3 shows that they earned more bonus based on their decisions (see also Table C1, which shows that there was a credible difference in performance). Figure 4 shows how well the different models capture participants' decisions. Interestingly, whereas in all previous conditions, the 'full' model captured participants' decisions best, experts' decisions were captured almost as well by the '∆P combined' model (see Table 3). The correlation between expert and novice decisions was r = .79. Figure 5 shows that, just like for novices, experts' decisions are predicted by their inferences. However, the relationship between inferences and decisions is slightly weaker in experts compared to novices.

Finally, we explored whether there were any differences in performance in our expert sample based on their degree (Table E1), or their self-rated familiarity with causal inference (Table E2). We found no credible differences.

Discussion

Expert participants recruited from Stanford in the economics, statistics, and data science departments made better decisions than participants recruited through a crowdsourcing platform online. However, interestingly, experts were slightly less accurate than novices in their inferences about the counterfactual types of people in the population. And, while their decisions were credibly better than those of novices, experts were still far from optimal. There were no credible differences in expert performance based on their degree (e.g., undergraduate vs. postdoc), or based on their self-reported familiarity with causal inference. Experts' decisions were very well-explained by the '∆P combined' model. This model first computes the differences in the probability of a positive outcome with and without the cause separately for the experimental group and the observational group, and then uses a linearly weighted combination of these difference scores to determine how to act.

General discussion

How do people make decisions based on experimental and observational data? We explored this question in three experiments, focusing on cases where these data logically imply a unique best action. Participants decided whether or not to hand out a flyer to a movie-goer at a theater. To decide well, participants needed to work out how likely the movie-goer was to be a complier (someone who goes because of the flyer), an always-goer, a never-goer, or a defier (someone who doesn't go because of the flyer), and then weigh each of these possibilities by what it was worth -the calculation prescribed by the counterfactual decision model (CDM; see Figure 1).

Participants' decisions were better than chance, but far from optimal. Receiving trial-by-trial feedback about the consequences of one's choice -including what would have happened had one chosen differently -didn't improve performance. Having participants engage more closely with the data before deciding helped, but only modestly. In Experiment 2, participants who first reported the composition of the data and those who first estimated the proportions of the four counterfactual types of movie-goers both earned credibly more bonus than participants in Experiment 1 (see Table C1), yet their accuracy still hovered just under 60%. Notably, simply having participants report the numbers in the table worked as well as having them reason explicitly about counterfactual types.

One possibility for the low performance is that participants simply ignored the observational data, as many people learn that experiments are the gold standard in science. If that had been the case, then their decisions would have been constant across scenarios that share the same experimental data, but they clearly weren't (see Figure 2). So while participants used both sources of information, they didn't follow the CDM's predictions. For example, scenarios B and C in Figure 2 imply the same expected benefit despite very different observational data, and participants were far more willing to hand out the flyer in B than in C. Scenarios D and E make the point even more sharply: the observational data is exactly reversed, the implied expected benefit is identical, and participants' decisions differed by roughly 40 percentage points. Across all conditions, participants' choices were best captured by weighted-additive models, and much less well by the CDM (see Table 3).

Experiment 2 shows that participants fail at the inference step (Figure 1B) rather than at the valuation step (Figure 1C). Participants' estimates of the proportions of compliers, always-goers, never-goers, and defiers bore almost no relationship to the CDM's normative predictions, r = .11 [-.10, .31]. Their inferences were not arbitrary thoughthey varied systematically with the data (see Table 4) -they were just wrong. Participants' inferences of the different counterfactual types were well-explained by models that combine the observational and experimental data in a linearly additive manner. Participants' decisions followed coherently from these incorrect inferences: the expected benefit computed from participants' estimates of the four types predicted their choices very well (see Figure 5). So, participants are doing the right thing with the wrong estimates.

Expertise didn't change this picture in the way we expected. The statistics, economics, and data science students in Experiment 3 made credibly better decisions than novices, earning more bonus. But their inferences about the four counterfactual types were no more accurate than those of novices -if anything slightly less so. Also, performance was unrelated to degree or to self-reported familiarity with causal inference. What distinguished experts was the heuristic they brought to bear: their decisions were well-explained by the '∆P combined' model, which computes a difference score separately within the experimental and the observational data and then combines the two. Experts, in other words, seem to have arrived at a better rule of thumb rather than at a better grasp of the counterfactual quantities.

Developing intuition

Let's try to develop a better intuition for how to correctly combine observational and experimental data to infer the different counterfactual types that make up the population. While Equation 1 provides the normative solution for inferring the probability that a person is a complier, this equation isn't particularly intuitive. Let us first summarize some of the key relationships here again:

Notice that these equations just use experimental data, and we've seen them all before (they are the same as Equations 2-4). Now the key to using them well is to identify which of the four counterfactual types the experimental and observational data constrain most directly.

Once we have a good sense for the probability of one of the counterfactual types, we can use the relationships above to infer the rest.

Let's consider the data from 'Apollo Theater' (Figure 6A). Here, the observational data provides a very strong constraint. In fact, it rules out never-goers, since everyone went. Given that we know that p(never-goer) = 0, we can infer that p(defier) = 0.5 (using Equation 9), then that p(complier) = 0.5 (using Equation 7; because p(y x ) -p(y x ′ ) = 0), and finally that p(always-goer) = 0 (using Equation 8). The observational data from 'Bacchus Theater' (Figure 6B) rules out defiers, because everyone with the flyer went, A flyer handed out flyer obtainable

and no one without the flyer went. Given that we know that p(defier) = 0, we can infer that p(never-goer) = 0.5 (using Equation 9), that p(complier) = 0 (using Equation 7), and that p(always-goer) = 0.5 (using Equation 8).

The observational data from 'Cupid Theater' (Figure 6C) rules out always-goers (no one went). Notice that this means that, somewhat surprisingly, the inferences about the different counterfactual types are the same at 'Cupid Theater' as they are at 'Apollo Theater', even though the observational data looks very different. Whereas at 'Apollo Theater', all the compliers took the flyer, and all the defiers didn't take the flyer, the opposite happened at 'Cupid Theater'. Here, the defiers took the flyer (so they didn't end up going), and the compliers didn't take the flyer (so they also didn't end up going). This situation might strike us as more unusual: why would the people whom a flyer dissuades take them, and those it persuades don't? One explanation is that the movie's title and flyer suggested different kinds of movies. The compliers found the title unappealing and skipped the flyer, even though it would have won them over, whereas the defiers were intrigued by the title, took a flyer, and were put off by its description. The counterfactual inferences at 'Dionysus Theater' (Figure 6D) and 'Bacchus Theater' are also the same. The data at 'Dionysus Theater' rules out compliers (no one with the flyer went, and everyone without the flyer went). At 'Bacchus Theater' all the always-goers took the flyer and the never-goers didn't take the flyer, whereas at 'Dionysus Theater', the always-goers didn't take the flyer and the never-goers took it.

Thanks to the logic of counterfactual inference, these four theaters were fairly easy to deal with. Things get a little more challenging when neither the observational nor the experimental data alone rule out one of the counterfactual types. Consider the data from 'Enlil Theater' (Figure 6E) and from 'Forseti Theater' (Figure 6F). The majority of participants made incorrect choices for both of these trials in all of the experiments. Notice that both feature the same experimental data but have different observational data.

Intuitively, handing out the flyer at 'Enlil Theater' seems like a good idea -and that's what a majority of participants did. Both the experimental data and the observational data appear to suggest that the flyer is helping. However, the expected benefit of handing out the flyer is actually negative. In contrast, handing out the flyer at 'Forseti Theater' seems like a bad idea -and the majority of participants didn't hand it out. However, here, the expected benefit is positive.

While the observational data at 'Enlil Theater' (Figure 6E) doesn't rule out any of the counterfactual types, it provides a strong constraint. We can see that the maximum probability of an always-goer is p(always-goer) ≤ 0.2 as only four out of twenty bought a ticket. So let's assume, for now, that p(always-goer) = 0.2 and infer what the rest of the probabilities would need to be. We can infer that p(complier) = 0.5 (using Equation 8), that p(defier) = 0.3 (using Equation 7), and that p(never-goer) = 0 (using Equation 9). While this is one possible solution, maybe there is another one? Let's assume that p(always-goer) = 0.1. From this we would get that p(complier) = 0.6, which means that p(defier) = 0.4 (using Equation 7). But notice that this doesn't work. We already have probabilities of these three types that sum to more than 1. The same reasoning holds if we were to try p(always-goer) = 0.15 or p(always-goer) = 0, for example. So we know that the first solution we found is the unique one. Let's try the same exercise with 'Forseti Theater' (Figure 6F). Here, based on the observational data, we know that p(complier) ≤ 0.2. Everyone who didn't take the flyer went (these can't be compliers), and only four out of ten who took the flyer went (these are either compliers or always-goers). From the fact that the average treatment effect is 0.2, we know that p(complier) = 0.2 and that p(defier) = 0 (using Equation 7). And we can use Equation 8and Equation 9 to infer that p(always-goer) = 0.5 and p(never-goer) = 0.3.

Overall, what this exercise shows is that it is possible to reason through the different cases to make informed inferences about the probability of the different counterfactual types of people. However, this reasoning doesn't come naturally to people. Instead, they rely on a simpler strategy that combines the observational and experimental data in a weighted additive way, leaving the experiment with much less money than they could have gotten.

Limitations and future directions

We explored participants' decisions and inferences in a single context -handing out flyers for movies. Future work should explore different decision contexts. It's possible, for example, that in our context, participants had strong prior beliefs that flyers are helpful. This might explain why they were overall somewhat biased to hand them out. In other contexts, people's prior beliefs might be different. Cinelli and Pearl (2021) develop a Bayesian approach that combines causal knowledge of the underlying mechanism with experimental and observational data to make good decisions. While it's possible that such an approach could help better understand participants' choices, the fact that their decisions were so well-explained by simple linear weighting suggests that they were relying on more heuristic reasoning.

Future work could also explore a greater range of situations. We focused here on a relatively simple setting that featured binary cause and effect variables, small data sets, and data for which the probabilities of the different counterfactual types can (almost always) be computed exactly, with the same benefit function throughout. Future work may want to explore how people make decisions with ordinal (Mueller, 2025; Sun, Shi, & Zhao, 2025) or continuous variables (Kawakami, Kuroki, & Tian, 2024; Li & Pearl, 2024). We assumed that our small data sets were a true reflection of the probabilities in the population. One could see whether participants' decisions are sensitive to sample size manipulations (T. Cheng, Mao, Pearl, & Li, 2026; Dawid, Musio, & Fienberg, 2016), including situations where the observational data isn't balanced between treatment and non-treatment. It would also be interesting to see how participants perform in more situations where it's only possible to compute bounds on the counterfactual probabilities. Finally, future work could manipulate the benefit parameters, making it, for example, so that the benefit of giving a flyer to a complier is greater than the harm of giving a flyer to a defier. Remember, however, that we found suboptimal performance in arguably one of the simplest settings. So it's plausible to assume that people would struggle even more in the extensions we suggested here. That said, future work could explore whether people can learn to make better decisions by receiving minimal instructions that elucidate how the counterfactual calculus works.

Conclusion

Doctors, managers, and policy makers often need to make decisions based on both experimental and observational data. Deciding well requires knowing more than whether an action works on average. It requires knowing whether it would work for the person in front of you -whether they would benefit, be harmed, or be left unaffected. Formal work tells us how to combine the two sources of data to answer that question. But without formal training, people are left to their intuitions. Those intuitions, we found, aren't up to the task. Even experts in statistics, economics, and data science left a lot of money on the table.

Much work has shown that people rely on heuristics and exhibit various biases when making decisions (Gilovich, Griffin, & Kahneman, 2002; Kahneman, 2011; see also Gigerenzer, Todd, ABC Research Group, et al., 2000). We have uncovered a new heuristic: when presented with experimental and observational data, people combine the available information using a simple additive weighting strategy. However, the correct solution requires a counterfactual calculus that implies a non-linear combination of the available information.

The source of the problem is a failure of inference, not of valuation. Give decisionmakers the right beliefs about who they are dealing with, and good decisions follow. Counterfactual reasoning is the bridge from the data to those beliefs -and, as our results suggest, a bridge that has to be taught rather than assumed. For the growing number of stakeholders who hold both experimental and observational data in hand, that training may be what separates a good decision from a costly one.
